title: Boolean Algebra and Digital Logic
short_intro: Boolean algebra is a branch of mathematics dealing with binary variables and logic operations used to analyze and simplify digital circuits. It forms the foundation of modern digital electronics, underpinning microprocessors, computer architecture, and gate-level logic design.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic logic gates (AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR, XNOR), truth tables, symbols, and fundamental Boolean postulates and laws.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: De Morgan's theorems, Karnaugh maps (K-maps) for simplification, Boolean expression minimization, realization of universal gates, and arithmetic circuits.

prerequisites: Binary number system and number base conversions
Basic concepts of voltage levels in digital electronics (TTL and CMOS)

concept_notes.heading: Fundamental Postulates of Boolean Algebra
bullets: Boolean variables take only two discrete values: logic 0 (false/LOW) and logic 1 (true/HIGH).
The basic operations are logical addition (OR, denoted by +), logical multiplication (AND, denoted by · or juxtaposition), and complementation (NOT, denoted by an overbar).
The commutative laws state that A + B = B + A and A · B = B · A.

concept_notes.heading: Basic Logic Gates and Truth Tables
bullets: The NOT gate (inverter) outputs the logical complement of its single input: Y = Ā.
The AND gate outputs HIGH (1) only when all its inputs are HIGH: Y = A · B.
The OR gate outputs HIGH (1) if at least one of its inputs is HIGH: Y = A + B.

concept_notes.heading: Universal Gates: NAND and NOR
bullets: A NAND gate is a combination of an AND gate followed by a NOT gate, with output Y = (A · B)̄.
A NOR gate is a combination of an OR gate followed by a NOT gate, with output Y = (A + B)̄.
NAND and NOR gates are termed universal gates because any boolean function can be implemented using only NAND gates or only NOR gates.

concept_notes.heading: De Morgan's Theorems
bullets: First Theorem: The complement of a sum is equal to the product of the complements, i.e., (A + B)̄ = Ā · B̄.
Second Theorem: The complement of a product is equal to the sum of the complements, i.e., (A · B)̄ = Ā + B̄.
These theorems are essential for converting sum-of-products (SOP) to product-of-sums (POS) forms and vice versa.

derivations.title: Simplification of Boolean Expression using Boolean Postulates
derivations.conditions: Simplify Y = AB + A(B + C) + B(B + C)
steps: Distribute terms: Y = AB + AB + AC + BB + BC
Apply idempotent law (BB = B and AB + AB = AB): Y = AB + AC + B + BC
Apply absorption law on B + BC (since B + BC = B): Y = AB + AC + B
Apply absorption law on AB + B (since AB + B = B): Y = B + AC
Apply distributive law or consensus if applicable; final reduced form is Y = B + AC

derivations.title: Realization of OR Gate using only NAND Gates
derivations.conditions: Expression to implement: Y = A + B using NAND logic
steps: Apply double complement to OR function: Y = (A + B)̄̄
Apply De Morgan's first theorem inside the inner complement: (A + B)̄ = Ā · B̄
Recognize that Ā is obtained by connecting input A to both terminals of a NAND gate, and similarly B̄.
The final output Y is obtained by feeding Ā and B̄ into a third NAND gate.

formula_sheet.name: AND Operation Law
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \cdot 0 = 0, \quad A \cdot 1 = A, \quad A \cdot A = A, \quad A \cdot A' = 0

formula_sheet.name: OR Operation Law
formula_sheet.equation_html: A + 0 = A, \quad A + 1 = 1, \quad A + A = A, \quad A + A' = 1

formula_sheet.name: Commutative Laws
formula_sheet.equation_html: A + B = B + A, \quad A \cdot B = B \cdot A

formula_sheet.name: Associative Laws
formula_sheet.equation_html: A + (B + C) = (A + B) + C, \quad A \cdot (B \cdot C) = (A \cdot B) \cdot C

formula_sheet.name: Distributive Laws
formula_sheet.equation_html: A \cdot (B + C) = A \cdot B + A \cdot C, \quad A + (B \cdot C) = (A + B) \cdot (A + C)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Timing Diagram for Logic Gates
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Square wave voltage pulses representing inputs A(t) and B(t) against time, with the corresponding output voltage pulse wave Y(t) for an AND or OR gate.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Visualizes the propagation delay and real-time response of digital gates to changing input levels.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Used in PGT questions to determine output waveforms given specific input pulse trains.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Transistor-Transistor Logic (TTL) NOT Gate Circuit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Circuit diagram featuring a multi-emitter npn transistor at the input stage followed by phase-splitter and totem-pole output driver transistors.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates how physical semiconductor devices implement digital inversion and voltage switching thresholds.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual understanding of hardware implementation of Boolean NOT operations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Karnaugh Map (K-map) Grid Structure
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A 2-variable or 4-variable grid arranged in Gray code sequence (00, 01, 11, 10) to map minterms for Boolean minimization.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Provides a pictorial method of grouping adjacent cells containing 1s to eliminate redundant literals.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested in PGT numericals for minimizing complex SOP expressions.

solved_numericals.question: Simplify the Boolean expression: Y = AB'C + ABC' + ABC + A'BC.
solution_steps: Group terms with common factors: Y = AC(B' + B) + BC(A + A')
Use the complement law (B' + B = 1 and A + A' = 1): Y = AC(1) + BC(1)

solved_numericals.question: Find the dual of the Boolean expression: X = AB + A'(B + C').
solution_steps: Recall that to find the dual of a Boolean expression, replace AND (.) with OR (+), OR (+) with AND (.), 0 with 1, and 1 with 0, leaving variables unchanged.
Original expression: X = AB + A'(B + C')
Replace '+' with '.' and '.' with '+': X_dual = (A + B) \cdot (A' + (B \cdot C''))
Note: Constants remain unchanged if present, variables retain their uncomplemented/complemented status.

solved_numericals.question: Using De Morgan's theorems, simplify the expression Y = ((A + B')' + C)'.
solution_steps: Apply De Morgan's second theorem to the outer complement: Y = (A + B')'' \cdot C'
Apply involution law ((A + B')'' = A + B'): Y = (A + B') \cdot C'
Expand the expression: Y = AC' + B'C'

assumptions_and_limitations: Assumption: Binary voltage levels are strictly categorized into two distinct states (Logic 0 and Logic 1) with instantaneous transitions. Limitation: Real physical circuits experience rise times, fall times, and propagation delays, and ambiguous voltage zones can cause erratic noise susceptibility.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Boolean addition (A + B) is equivalent to arithmetic addition (1 + 1 = 2).
common_misconceptions.correct: Boolean addition represents logical OR, where 1 + 1 = 1.
common_misconceptions.why: Boolean algebra operates on a two-valued domain {0, 1} where maximum logical truth is 1.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The dual of an expression is the same as its complement.
common_misconceptions.correct: The dual interchanges AND and OR operators, whereas the complement interchanges operators AND/OR and also inverts all variables (A to A').
common_misconceptions.why: Duality is based on operator interchange, while complementation applies De Morgan's laws fully.

quick_revision: Boolean algebra uses variables restricted to two states: 0 and 1, governed by OR (+), AND (.), and NOT (') operations.
AND Operation Law: A \cdot 0 = 0, \quad A \cdot 1 = A, \quad A \cdot A = A, \quad A \cdot A' = 0
OR Operation Law: A + 0 = A, \quad A + 1 = 1, \quad A + A = A, \quad A + A' = 1
